provenance.method: gap = |goal - baseline| directionally; recovered = |after - baseline| directionally; remaining = gap - recovered; goal_met = remaining <= 0 (PLAN §4.1 Improve-loop gap arithmetic, rubric R-IMP-04, BoK IV.C.1)

artifact.notes: The measurement stop is told as a finding, not an embarrassment: round-1 kappa, the fix, round 2, and the baseline that came back HIGHER than the broken pre-log.

panels.narrative: Patrons and desk staff report the catalog says a book is on the shelf and it isn't there. An informal closers' log suggested ~3.8% -- but the two counters had never agreed on a definition (a fingerprint hiding in the logged_by column).

The measurement stop: T-12 round 1 failed (kappa 0.336, EXIT-02) -- the run stopped, no baseline, no chart. After the written-definition fix, round 2 passed (kappa 0.878), and the baseline came back HIGHER than the broken log: p-bar 0.0653 (stable, 21 subgroups), not the pre-log's ~3.8% -- the broken gauge had hidden roughly two-fifths of the problem.
Halve the audited misshelve proportion from 0.0653 to 0.0326 by 2026-11-30, without dropping shelving throughput more than 10%.

Out-of-order-within-bay (48.9%) and wrong-bay (32.2%) are the engine-verified 81.1% vital few. Root cause: sorting happens at the shelf, on a room with no sortable standard -- the section chi-square screen shows juvenile hit hardest, where series conventions bite.
Pre-sorted carts + posted standard ranked first, directly at the verified root; double-checking at the shelf and a training-only workshop both ranked lower (symptom, not root).

Settled-weeks two-proportion z: baseline vs settled weeks, z=4.01, p=6.0e-05 -- significant. Full 24-day after window: threshold met (rate under 4.0%), verdict weakened by the declared fall reading-program confound (direction: can only push the rate up). Gap recovery over 100% of the halving goal.

p-chart limits history on one artifact: baseline freeze, the improvement arriving as a rule-4 run on the old limits, then a logged recalculation on the 24-day post window. Control plan monitors the rate weekly, throughput, and the method itself; Ruth Delgado accepted the owner role 2026-11-04. Quarterly kappa re-run guards the definition.

The measurement stop is the project's real lesson: a plausible-looking log would have frozen a ~3.8% baseline nobody could trust, and every downstream number would have inherited an unchecked gauge. Stopping at EXIT-02, fixing the definition, and re-baselining found a HIGHER, honest number -- the strongest argument for having stopped.

questions.text: Is the problem stated in measurable terms, with no cause and no fix implied?
Does the charter name a process owner who has actually agreed to the scope?
Is the business impact stated in dollars or hours, and does it hold up against an independent number?
Is the baseline built on a process the data shows is stable, not just assumed to be?
Has the measurement system itself been checked, and did it pass?
Is the operational definition tight enough that two different people would measure the same thing the same way?
Does every candidate cause carry actual evidence, not just an opinion in the room?
Are the verified causes the ones the data points to, not just the easiest ones to fix?
Has every severity-9/10 failure mode been given an action, not just logged and left?
Was exactly one change piloted at a time, with a success threshold set before the data came in?
Does the before/after proof account honestly for anything else that changed during the pilot?
How much of the original gap does this fix close, and what is the plan for what's left?
Does every monitored item have a real, named owner who has accepted the role?
Is there an out-of-control response path a person could actually follow, today, without asking what it means?
Is someone trained on the new method, by name, with a way to verify they can actually do it?
Does the realized benefit trace to the measured improvement, not to the original COPQ hope?
Are the lessons learned substantive, including at least one thing that didn't work?
Is every open item handed off to a named owner, not left to fall through?
